# Second Brain V5 — anchored memory that proves it helps

## 0. The one-paragraph version

V4 made the Brain small, fast and felt: a start card, a working state that survives compaction,
one known fix on a failure, recall and note in one call. The first live week says which of those
earn their tokens. The start card (the plan carried across sessions and restarts) and known fixes
do; the post-compaction resume repeated what OMP's own summary already kept; recall mostly
answers the wrong question; the learning loop has not produced one accepted note. V5 changes
three things and puts two more on trial. First, **anchors instead of copies**: the working state
and recall point into the repo's own plan documents (`docs/LOOP.md › Resume`) and render their
current text, so the Brain can never drift from the repo it summarises. Second, **recall judged
on real agent queries**: a second frozen eval built from logged `brain_recall` calls, where a
wrong answer costs more than silence. Third, **learning that lands**: every fired fix is scored
by whether the next attempt succeeded, and pair mining is replaced by one measured end-of-task
prompt. On trial: kits and the post-compaction resume, each kept only if a longer benchmark shows
a benefit. Anything that still produces nothing after two weeks is deleted.

## 2. Diagnosis

1. **Compaction continuity is not where the resume earns its tokens yet.** In a short scripted
   session, OMP's own summary carried goal and next every time; removing the 57-token resume
   changed nothing. The card is what carries the plan across sessions, restarts and machines.
   Whether the resume matters in long sessions (several compactions, a summary crowded with other
   work) is unmeasured.
2. **Recall answers questions the Brain cannot know.** Agents query in keyword bags about project
   knowledge ("LOOP.md goals", "jobq commands", "sealed.py rewrite …"). That knowledge lives in
   the repo's documents, not in 160 notes, so BM25 over notes either stays silent or matches one
   shared word. The frozen eval did not see this: its prompts are V3-era natural-language
   questions whose answers *are* notes.
3. **The working state duplicates the repo's plan.** Projects with a living plan file
   (`docs/LOOP.md`, this repo's plan §6.1) get a second, shorter copy in `work/<project>.md`.
   "The repo wins on conflict" is a rule the agent must apply by hand, every session.
4. **The learning loop does not close.** Pair mining finds command retries, but real repairs are
   edits; every proposal so far was noise. Agents write notes when asked (40), rarely unprompted.
   Nothing measures whether a note or fix, once shown, helped.

## 3. What changes

### 3.1 Anchors, not copies

- `projects.json` gains `docs`: plan files the Brain may read (default: none; `brain project docs
  add docs/LOOP.md`). Only Markdown headings and the text under one heading are ever read; code is
  never indexed.
- `brain_state` accepts an anchor line, `See: docs/LOOP.md#resume`. The card renders that section's
  **current** text from the checkout (cut to the state's budget, ≤ 150 tokens after compaction)
  instead of a stored copy; the stored text is only the delta the file does not hold. A missing
  file or heading shows `anchor missing: docs/LOOP.md#resume` once, never a stale copy.
- Recall that finds no note answers with at most one heading line from the project's `docs`:
  `docs/LOOP.md › Goals (line 12)`. Budget unchanged: ≤ 3 lines.

Done when: in this repo and Absolute Laya, the card's "where we left off" equals the anchored
section byte-for-byte after an edit to the file, with no `brain_state` call; `LOOP.md goals`
answers with the heading line.

### 3.2 Recall judged on real queries

- Telemetry keeps each recall's query (scrubbed, local `state/` only) and the ids it returned.
- A second frozen eval, `test/fixtures/recall-real.jsonl`, from the logged queries (the 37 above
  plus two weeks of new ones), each labelled with its right note, heading, or "silence".
- Gate: wrong answers ≤ 10 % of queries; right answers never fewer than the day the set is frozen;
  the V3 eval keeps its thresholds.

Done when: both evals run in the gate and `brain stats` shows the weekly wrong-answer rate from a
labelled sample.

### 3.3 Learning that lands

- **Fix efficacy.** When a known fix fires, the next run of the same command (or tool) within the
  session decides it: success → `helped`, failure → `missed`. `brain stats` shows helped/missed per
  fix; a fix below 50 % over ≥ 4 firings loses `tested` and says so on `brain review`.
- **One end-of-task prompt, measured.** `BRAIN_STOP_NUDGE` (built in V4, off) runs in agentbench
  on vs off; it ships only if it raises notes that are later recalled or fired without costing
  more than 5 % tokens.
- **Pair mining gets two weeks.** If no capture proposal is accepted by then, capture proposals
  (not the event log, which feeds fixes and stats) are deleted.

Done when: every fired fix has an outcome in telemetry; the nudge has a shipped/rejected verdict
with numbers; capture proposals are either producing accepted notes or gone.

### 3.4 Kits: confirm or fold

With the kit body in the recall answer, the kit beat native narrowly (6 + 6 runs: −2 % tokens,
−3 % calls, −25 % cost to first pass). One more task shape and 12 + 12 runs decide it: if the
advantage does not hold, a kit becomes a `procedure` note (recall already returns bodies) and
`kits/`, `brain kit …` and the card's kit line are deleted.

### 3.5 Resume: prove it or trim it

compactbench gains a long-session scenario: three compactions, each turn crowded with unrelated
reads and edits, the goal changed once midway. `resume` vs `ablate`, 10 + 10. If removing the
resume still changes nothing, the post-compaction resume carries only what the host summary
dropped (edited files, the last failure) or is removed; the start card is untouched.

### 3.6 Sign-off and host parity (carried from V4)

A week of daily use; P6 cleanup; the `v2-archive` tag pushed on the owner's go; Claude Code
verified end to end once the owner's Claude login is renewed (the hook already delivers the card).

## 4. What V5 does not do

No embeddings, no database, no code indexing, no new resident tools (still three), no per-prompt
injection, no second harness adapter beyond the Claude Code hook and MCP. The card stays ≤ 400
tokens and appears once per session (after compaction only its lean line, ~35 tokens: the state
part is not repeated, §8 P4; the lean rule is behaviour the rest of the session still needs).

### 8.1 Recall precision (2026-09-28, owner: "as close to 0% wrong as possible")

Labels were redone blind: three independent judges saw each logged query, what the agent did next,
and the top-10 candidates in id order (never the tool's answer); the majority label is ground
truth (`recall-real.jsonl`, 34 frozen; `recall-real-heldout.jsonl`, 20 logged after the freeze).
A wrong answer now counts any irrelevant note shown, including one beside a relevant note.
Word matching alone could not separate relevant from irrelevant hits (they overlap on every lexical
signal), so recall now checks its lexical answer with TypeSafe Jev and drops notes and plan-doc
headings below 0.75 (owner decision; fail open to the lexical answer; private notes never sent).

| Set | Lexical right / wrong / missed | Judged right / wrong / missed |
|---|---|---|
| Frozen 34 | 6 / 8 / 7 | 7 / **0** / 12 |
| Held-out 20 | 2 / 4 / 4 | 3 / **0** / 5 |
| V3 dev / held-out | 13/15, 7/8 | 13/15, 8/8 (gate lowered to 12/15 for D27 at 0.45) |

Live calls: ~300 ms (5 s timeout). The price is more silence: some useful notes score just
under 0.75 and are dropped. Next: keep logging real queries; re-label and re-measure held-out
monthly so 0 wrong is checked on queries the threshold never saw.

### 8.2 Judge robustness and call-time context (2026-09-28)

**Drift.** The same 54 real queries re-scored three more times: Jev moves about ±0.02 per pair
(mean |Δ| 0.016), enough to flip borderline notes. At 0.75 the reruns showed 1, 2 and 1 wrong
answers (the first recording, 0, was lucky). At **0.78** all four runs had 0 wrong; right answers
fall from 6–7 to 5–6 (frozen) and 2–3 to 2–3 (held-out); V3 dev 12/15 (D28 "migration" sits at
0.75–0.78). Threshold raised to 0.78; the eval now requires 0 wrong on every recorded run
(`recall-judge-reruns.json`).

**Agent context in the judge: rejected.** Hypothesis: misses happen because the judge sees only the
keyword query, while the labellers saw what the agent was doing. On the 40 queries with a logged
call-time intent (`i`) and user task, one batch: AUC query-only 0.904, + intent 0.900, + intent
and task 0.915. The differences are one case each way, inside run-to-run noise, and sending the
user's task text adds exposure for no measured gain. Not shipped.

**What limits recall now** is not the judge but coverage: of 13 frozen misses, most have their
relevant note scoring 0.4–0.7 on a keyword query. Next lever to test: ask agents (tool
description) for a one-sentence question instead of a keyword list, measured by agentbench.

Miss breakdown at 0.78 (first rerun): 18 labelled-relevant misses; 11 never reach the lexical
answer and 7 are shown but judged below 0.78. Of the 11, only one (H04, 0.84) would pass the judge
if the whole top-10 were judged; the rest score 0.14–0.74 on their keyword query. Widening the
shortlist therefore buys one answer; the query text itself is the ceiling.

### 8.5 Borrowed from OKF: expiry, verifier, export (2026-10-04)

Owner asked for the best parts of Google's Open Knowledge Format v0.2 (markdown + YAML
frontmatter bundles; github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/open-knowledge-format). OKF stays an export
format, not the canonical one: its data-catalog fields (attested computations, usage counts) have
no use here, and v0.2 is young. D4 gains three optional keys; nothing else changes.

- **`stale_after`** (OKF §5.5): a date (start of day, UTC) or ISO instant with an offset. Past
  it, a note is stale everywhere: recall sorts it last and marks `(stale since <date>)`, the card
  applies the stale-evidence −3, and it is never pushed as a known fix (an author-stated expiry,
  unlike missing evidence, is not a guess). Set with `brain note --stale-after`; not a
  `brain_note` parameter: tried as agentbench arm `v5-staleafter` (learn, 6 + 6, same batch):
  +18 % A+B tokens, +12 % cost, landed 4 → 3, and no agent ever set it (0/6). Arm deleted.
- **`tested_by` / `tested_at`** (OKF `verified`, §5.2–5.3): who verified a tested note and when:
  `agent` (`brain_note`/`brain note --tested`), `capture` (an accepted fail→pass proposal),
  `owner` (`brain tested <id>`, which re-stamps), `convert` (V3 grade). The first verifier sticks
  on re-notes. Shown on explicit id reads; gating and ranking unchanged. Older tested notes stay
  unrecorded.
- **`brain export <dir>`**: public notes as an OKF 0.2 bundle (concept per note, `index.md` per
  folder, `okf_version` at the root). `kind` → `type`, `source` → `generated.by`, `tested_by` →
  `verified.by` (`human:owner` only for `owner`), `retired` → `status: deprecated` plus lineage
  links, file evidence → a "<path> in the <project> checkout" source. Private notes never
  exported; the target must be empty or an earlier export, outside the home except `state/`.
  Live home (2026-10-04): 319 notes, all frontmatter valid YAML.

# Second Brain V4 — the agent-experience overhaul

## 0. The one-paragraph version

Second Brain becomes a small TypeScript library with two faces: an **Oh My Pi extension** that runs
it in-process, and a **`brain` CLI** for any other shell or harness. It stores plain Markdown files
in a git repo. It does exactly five things an agent can feel: a **start card** at session start,
**continuity** across compaction (the agent's own working state survives and comes back), **recall**
and **note** in one call each, **one known fix** when a tool fails, and **kits** — proven paths from
earlier projects that get a new MVP up with the least exploration. Everything that does not show up
in a session is deleted: no grades, no promotion ceremony, no constitution, no ledgers, no
qualification campaigns, no SQLite, no Python, no migrations.

## 1. Diagnosis — where it went wrong

| What the repo optimised for | What an agent actually feels |
|---|---|
| Provability: constitution, sealed approvals, ledger chains, evidence manifests, "authority laundering" rules, qualification campaigns (116 MB of `outputs/`) | Nothing. None of it changes a single token an agent sees. |
| Vocabulary: candidate → current, promote, grade (claimed vs effective), conflict, supersession kinds, doctor | Friction: `brain add "…" --type gotcha --evidence …` then `brain promote --reason …` before it is even pushed. The agent writes nothing. |
| 68 Python modules (54k lines), 28 migrations, a 22-module OMP extension (2.7k lines), five harness adapters | A venv, `PYTHONHOME` breakage, process spawns per hook, four adapters nobody uses. |
| V3 (4.7k lines) fixed the *per-prompt noise* and the *import graph*, but kept the governance vocabulary | The real gap stayed open: after compaction the agent gets the **project brief** back, not **what it was doing**. Working state is still lost. |

The corpus itself is the tell: **113 of 120 records are `fact`**, 95 are still `candidate`. The
machinery for grades and promotion has almost nothing to grade. Meanwhile the moment that hurts
most — compaction mid-task — has no record type at all.

## 2. What "good" feels like (the design target)

Every feature below is defined as an agent moment with a token budget. If a feature has no
moment, it is not built.

| Moment | The agent gets | Budget |
|---|---|---|
| **Session start** | One *card*: what this project is (3 lines), where we left off (goal · done · next · watch out), the 5 most relevant truths, pending proposals count, matching kits | ≤ 400 tokens |
| **Working** | `brain_note("…")` and `brain_recall("…")`, one argument each. `brain_state("…")` to rewrite where-we-are. No output unless asked. | recall ≤ 3 lines; writes return one line |
| **Compaction** | Nothing lost that matters: the working state (agent-written, auto-completed with files touched and the last failing command) is snapshotted before compaction and re-injected right after | ≤ 150 tokens re-injected |
| **Tool failure** | One known fix if a *tested* note matches the error; otherwise nothing | ≤ 80 tokens |
| **New project / MVP** | A *kit*: stack decision with the why, scaffold commands, gotchas, "MVP done" checklist — from projects that already did it | one file, ≤ 600 tokens |
| **Ordinary prompt** | Nothing | 0 |

Two numbers we hold ourselves to on the owner's machine, in OMP, measured not argued:
1. **Continuity:** after a forced compaction mid-task, the agent states goal and next step
   correctly without re-reading files — 10 of 10 scripted runs.
2. **Neutrality + value:** on the slim task suite, tasks that need memory cost fewer tokens and tool
   calls than native; tasks that do not need it cost the same (±2 %).

> **Assumption A1 ("ponytail").** I read *"act like ponytail in which we could design MVPs for
> projects in least amount of tokens"* as: a fast, reusable path from idea to running MVP. That is
> the **kits** feature (§4.5). If ponytail is a specific tool or pattern you have in mind, name it
> and §4.5 changes; nothing else in the plan depends on it.

## 3. Architecture

```text
~/.omp/agent/extensions/second-brain/   (thin: hooks + 3 tools, imports the library)
                       │ in-process, 0 spawn
                       ▼
             brain/  (TypeScript library, Node built-ins only)
               ├─ store    read/write Markdown notes, working state, kits
               ├─ search   in-memory BM25 over title · tags · body (corpus ≈ 150 KB → < 5 ms)
               ├─ card     start card / resume card, hard budgets
               ├─ capture  failed → fixed pairs → proposals; error → known fix
               └─ sync     git add/commit/pull --rebase/push of the Brain home
                       ▲
             brain CLI (same functions; any shell, any harness; Claude Code hook = 40 lines)

Brain home (a git repo)
  notes/<project>/*.md      durable notes, one per file          synced
  notes/global/*.md         cross-project notes and gotchas      synced
  kits/<name>/SKILL.md      MVP kits, Agent-Skills format        synced
  state/<project>/working.md  goal · done · next · watch out      synced (tiny)
  state/events/*.jsonl      tool-result log for capture          local only
  projects.toml             id → paths / git remote / tags       synced
```

### 3.1 Decisions (and what they kill)

| # | Decision | Why | Kills |
|---|---|---|---|
| **D1** | **TypeScript, drop Python** | OMP is TypeScript: the extension calls the library in-process — no spawn, no venv, no `PYTHONHOME`. One language, one test runner. Harness independence is kept by the `brain` CLI (Node is already required by OMP). | 54k lines of Python, the venv, `bootstrap.ps1`, `brainctl.cmd`, pyright/ruff/pytest |
| **D2** | **No database** | 120–2 000 notes is ≈ 0.15–3 MB. Load all and score in memory in single-digit ms. No index to rebuild, no lock, no corruption, no `node:sqlite` availability question. Re-evaluate only above ~5 000 notes (measured, not assumed). | SQLite, FTS5, 28 migrations, `brain index`, `brain views`, the derived-views problem class |
| **D3** | **Three resident tools in OMP** (`brain_recall`, `brain_note`, `brain_state`) | V3 refused resident schemas to save tokens per turn. With prompt caching the schema (~250 tokens total) is paid once per context, while a bash round-trip to `brain q` costs more *per call* and is easy for the agent to skip. One-argument tools get used; CLIs get forgotten. Configurable off for hook-only mode. | the "discovery line in AGENTS.md" workaround |
| **D4** | **Notes, not records.** Frontmatter: `id, kind, project|global, tags, at, source, tested?, evidence?, replaces?, retired?` | Everything an agent or the capture path can fill in one call. `tested` gates what gets pushed on errors; `evidence` (optional paths) gates staleness; `replaces` keeps history. | status ladder, grades, promote, conflict, supersession kinds, doctor's integrity suite |
| **D5** | **Working state is a first-class file** the agent owns | The compaction gap. The harness's summary is lossy and not ours; `working.md` is deterministic, budgeted and re-injected. Also the resume card next session and the cross-machine handoff. | handoff envelopes, capsules, ledgers, active-state mirrors |
| **D6** | **Kits are Agent Skills** (`SKILL.md`) | Loadable natively by OMP and Claude Code; no new format; cross-project by nature. Drafted from a project's notes by `brain kit new`, finished by hand. | the skills lifecycle (candidate/shadow/staged/active/quarantine), skill evals, skillforge |
| **D7** | **Silence and budgets are code, not policy** | Every push path truncates to its budget and refuses to add on ordinary prompts. Telemetry line per session: tokens injected, brain tool calls, ms. | per-prompt autoinject, injection slots, recall gates |
| **D8** | **OMP is the host in focus; independence through the CLI**, not through adapters | One extension, one CLI, one optional 40-line Claude Code hook. | Antigravity, Hermes, Codex adapters, the legacy Claude Code adapter |

### 3.2 Rules (binding for V4 work)

1. A feature exists only if it has a moment in §2 and shows up in telemetry as used within a
   week of daily use. Otherwise it is deleted, not deprecated.
2. Writes take one argument. Anything that needs a flag to be useful is designed wrong.
3. Budgets are enforced in code (truncate, then refuse), never in a document.
4. The Brain never blocks, vetoes, steers or continues host work. It adds context or nothing.
   *`BRAIN_STOP_NUDGE` exception withdrawn: measured and deleted (V5 §8 P3, `421beaa`).*
5. Files are the truth. Anything derived is rebuilt from files on start; nothing derived is
   committed.
6. Node built-ins only in the library and the extension. No dependency is added without a
   measured need.
7. Nothing the Brain stores grants permission or authority; every injected line is advisory.
8. Private notes (`notes/**/private/`) never leave the machine; the sync path excludes them by
   pathspec, not by convention.

## 4. Features

### 4.1 Start card (`brain card`, `before_agent_start`)

Assembled from: project summary (first 3 lines of `notes/<project>/README.md` or projects.toml
description) · `state/<project>/working.md` · top-5 notes by a fixed ranking (tested gotchas for
this project, then recent decisions, then facts touched in the last 30 days) · `N proposals
pending` · `kits: a, b` when the project's tags match a kit. Hidden custom message
(`brain.card`), once per session and once after each compaction. Under 400 tokens by
construction: sections are filled greedily and cut.

### 4.2 Continuity (`brain_state`, `session_before_compact`, `session_compact`)

- The agent rewrites `working.md` with `brain_state("Goal … / Done … / Next … / Watch out …")`
  whenever the plan changes. Free Markdown, truncated to 150 tokens.
- Before compaction the extension auto-completes the state from the tool log: files edited, the
  last failing command, the last user prompt — only the fields the agent left empty, ≤ 80 tokens.
- After compaction the state is delivered as the next turn's hidden context
  (`sendMessage(…, { deliverAs: "nextTurn" })`), together with the card if the session is new.
- Session end writes a one-line `last session:` into the state, which becomes tomorrow's resume.

### 4.3 Recall and note (`brain_recall`, `brain_note`, CLI `brain recall|note`)

- Recall: BM25 over title (×5), tags (×3), body (×1); project first, then global and shared tags;
  relative floor 0.5 of the best hit; ≤ 3 lines, or nothing. `--all` widens to every project.
  The V3 ranking already gets 13/15 dev and 7/8 held-out on the frozen cases; V4 must not regress.
- Note: `brain_note("text")` → `notes/<project>/<id>.md` with `kind: note`, `source: agent`,
  `at: now`. Optional `kind: decision|gotcha|fact|procedure`, optional `tags`. Returns the id.
  A gotcha with an error line becomes a candidate correction; it is pushed on matching errors only
  after `tested: true` (set by `brain note --tested <id>` or automatically when capture sees the
  fix work).

### 4.4 Capture and known fixes (`tool_result`, `brain review`)

- The extension appends every tool result to `state/events/<session>.jsonl` (Brain-owned format,
  5 MB cap, 14-day retention). Port of the V3 logger.
- `brain review` turns failed → fixed pairs (same program, later success) and `Brain-Decision:` /
  `Brain-Gotcha:` commit trailers into proposals; secrets scrubbed; accept/reject in one command.
  The card shows the pending count and nothing more.
- On `tool_result` with `isError`, one tested note whose error pattern matches is appended to
  the result (≤ 80 tokens). Port of the V3 correction path.

### 4.5 Kits — MVPs in the fewest tokens (`brain kit`)

A kit is `kits/<name>/SKILL.md`: **when to use**, **stack decision and why**, **scaffold steps**
(exact commands, in order), **gotchas** (each with the failing symptom), **MVP-done checklist**.
≤ 600 tokens.

- `brain kit new <name> --from <project>` drafts a kit from that project's decisions, procedures
  and tested gotchas; you finish it by hand. `brain kit list`, `brain kit show`.
- The card names matching kits (by project tags); `brain_recall("kit fastapi")` returns one.
- Kits are cross-project by definition and load natively as skills in OMP and Claude Code.
- Value is measured, not assumed: scaffolding a fresh project with the kit versus native, tokens
  and tool calls to first passing run.

### 4.6 Cross-project and sync (`brain sync`)

`notes/global/` and shared tags (`projects.toml`) give cross-project visibility without moving
files. `brain sync` = commit the Brain paths (excluding private), pull `--rebase --autostash`,
push. Port of V3 sync. Working state syncs too, so a laptop can resume a desktop's task.

### 4.7 Other harnesses

`brain card` and `brain recall` are the whole contract. A Claude Code adapter is one hook script
(`SessionStart` → card, `PostToolUseFailure` → known fix) of ~40 lines, shipped but not in focus.

## 5. Kill list (from `main`, after P2 is live — see D-owner-5)

Everything is preserved in history under the tag `v2-archive`; `main` is rebuilt as the V4 tree.

- `src/second_brain/` (all 68 modules incl. `kb/` once ported), `pyproject.toml`, `.venv` scripts,
  `brainctl.*`, `scripts/*.ps1` except the new installer, all `tests/test_*.py`.
- `brainstem/prime-extension/` (legacy extension), `brainstem/adapters/*`, `brainstem/codex-hooks`.
- `constitution/`, `engrams/`, `experiences/`, `decisions/`, `plasticity/`, `sleep/`, `skills/*`
  lifecycle dirs, `memory/` (legacy store — converted to notes first), `db/`.
- `outputs/` (116 MB), `docs/intake/*` campaigns, mandates, registers and evidence; `docs/superpowers`,
  `docs/components`, `docs/architecture` (rewritten from scratch as one page).
- CI becomes: eslint · `tsc --noEmit` · vitest · a 2-minute eval smoke.

What is carried over (ported, not rewritten): the 120 records → notes (frontmatter trimmed by a
one-shot converter), the search ranking and its frozen case sets, the capture/scrub/correction
logic, the git sync, the event logger, the slim value suite (runner + tasks only), the two
frozen S2 case sets.

# BasicUpscaler plan

Project priorities, feature names and milestone order now live in
[ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md). This file retains engineering budgets, quality rules,
known bugs and training constraints. Use [the documentation index](docs/README.md)
for detailed feature evidence. Historical results below keep their original scope;
verify the current display configuration rather than assuming the older 60 Hz setup.

## Goal

Our own powerful, efficient and reliable algorithms, each shipped in one app:

| | Games (live window) | Videos (files, or a player via live capture) | Images |
|---|---|---|---|
| Upscaler | yes | yes | yes |
| Frame generation | yes | yes | — |
| Frame pacer | yes | — (cadence is solved by frame generation to the display rate) | — |

Target machine: RTX 5070 Ti Laptop (12 GB), 16 GB RAM, panel 1920×1200, rated 165 Hz but
running at 60 Hz (the owner no longer has 165 Hz, 28 Sep; plan for 60 Hz).
Live output always fills the panel. Games that follow their window render the panel's
16:10 shape (Game window); games locked to 16:9 use Screen fill, Smart by default.

Test games: Dragon Ball Sparking! ZERO, Bloons TD 6 (mouse-driven), Brawlhalla,
Granblue Fantasy Relink.

## How we get gains

Every algorithm competes in the **arena** (`arena/`): fixed datasets, fixed metrics,
one scoreboard (`SCOREBOARD.md`, generated). A candidate enters the app only if it

- beats the current champion on quality within the cost budget, or
- matches the champion's quality at lower cost.

Quality: see "What a good upscaled image is" below. Cost: GPU ms on the 5070 Ti at the
target size, and VRAM.

**Baselines (owner, 28 Sep).** Two, never mixed in one table (DECISIONS 14):

- **Same inputs — FSR1** (EASU + RCAS): AMD's newest non-ML *spatial* upscaler and our
  in-app champion. Every capture-based candidate must beat it on the same frames.
- **Reference — FSR 3.1.5**: AMD's newest non-ML upscaler (temporal; FidelityFX SDK
  v2.3.0, MIT source). It needs the renderer's jittered colour, depth and motion vectors,
  so it cannot run on captured frames; it runs in an offline research renderer (AMD
  Capsaicin v1.3, which integrates it) on scenes rendered three ways: native truth,
  FSR 3.1.5, and the plain low-res frame a game would present. It measures how far
  capture-based upscaling is from the best non-ML result a game can integrate. FSR 3's
  optical flow (colour-only, 8×8 blocks, scene-cut flag) is the baseline for our motion
  core (P2) and frame generation (P3/P4).

Budgets (owner may change): live upscale ≤ 3 ms per frame to the panel; frame
generation ≤ 4 ms per generated frame; added display latency without frame
generation ≤ one refresh (6.06 ms at 165 Hz; 16.7 ms at the 60 Hz the panel now runs) plus
our GPU time, versus the same game unscaled.

Where P0 stands against them (28 Sep 2026, `arena.latency`, 1280×720 60 fps test source,
repeated runs with a stage split): upscale to 1920×1080 costs 0.02 ms (bilinear) to
0.18 ms (FSR1) of GPU — well inside 3 ms. Our own loop is negligible (frame taken 0.01 ms
after it arrives, presented 0.1 ms later; on screen 1.8 ms after that without vsync).
Almost all added delay is **Windows' capture, which happens once per screen refresh**: a
game frame waits for the next composition, 0–1 refresh, with a random phase that is fixed
for the session (runs of the same build ranged 2–18 ms). **The panel runs at 60 Hz**
(driver offers only 30/48/60 Hz; G-Helper `screen_max = 60`; 165 Hz is no longer available
to the owner), so that wait is up to 16.7 ms. **Vsync is the largest cost we control:**
Smart, 60 Hz, five runs each — vsync on +42 ms added (median; 23–46), vsync off +14 ms.
Half of the vsync cost was a stale-frame rhythm, now fixed by `VsyncPacer` (Known bugs):
frame arrival to screen is 15.4 ms with vsync (one refresh) and 1.8 ms without.

## What a good upscaled image is

Sources: `../BasicUpscaler Research/Image Quality/` (01 photography and human vision, 02
upscaled-image quality and measurement, 28 Sep 2026, every claim linked to a primary source).

**Definition.** A good upscale keeps the game's intended shapes, text, colours, tones and
real texture, at the size and speed it is actually watched, without visible artifacts
(halos, jaggies, false detail, shimmer). Looking sharper is not the goal by itself:
sharpening can add edge contrast without adding information, and "sharper", "more
saturated", "less noisy" or "higher average score" are each not enough to call it better.

**Viewing geometry.** 16-inch 1920×1200 panel: 141.5 ppi. At 60 cm one pixel is 1.03
arcminutes (58 pixels per degree), so one- and two-pixel halos are not automatically
invisible. Human contrast sensitivity peaks around 3–5 cycles/degree, i.e. features
12–19 output pixels per cycle here: medium-scale contrast errors and wide halos matter,
not only the finest detail. Assumed distance, not measured.

**What decides quality, in priority order for our games** (proposed ranking, not a
published one; any severe failure overrides it):

1. Geometry and outlines intact: aspect, line width, no broken or merged strokes.
2. Stable in motion: no shimmer or crawling edges when the camera pans slowly.
3. HUD and text readable: glyphs, numbers and icons keep their shape.
4. No halos, ringing or staircasing on edges.
5. Real sharpness, not edge exaggeration.
6. Tones kept: no new clipping, shadows and highlights separated as in the source.
7. Colours kept, including thin coloured strokes (Y-only metrics miss these).
8. Clean flat fills and smooth gradients: no banding or blotches.
9. Real texture kept, not smoothed away or invented.
10. No added noise.

**How the arena changes** (work items; P0 rows where cheap, the rest before P1 promotion):

- Keep PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS for continuity; add NVIDIA **FLIP** (mean, with the real viewing
  distance; official CLI, as there is no Python 3.14 wheel) and **DISTS** for texture
  audits. No single averaged score; FLIP p95 and error maps show localized defects.
- **Diagnostic chart set** with known truth: slanted edges (grey 0.1→0.9 so clipping
  cannot hide overshoot), zone plates and frequency sweeps, thin lines of 0.5–2 source
  pixels at 0/¼/½/¾-pixel phases, text/HUD sheets, cel-style outlines on flat fills,
  smooth ramps, chroma-only edges, and all of them moving at ¼–2 pixels per frame.
  Report overshoot/undershoot ÷ edge contrast, halo width, edge width, line-width and
  position error, false-frequency response, and temporal instability (tLPIPS as TecoGAN
  defines it, plus motion-compensated residual change).
- **Separate gates, not averaged in:** HUD/text damage, broken outlines, shimmer and cost
  each reject a candidate on their own.
- **Game ground truth is the game rendered natively at the higher resolution**, not a
  downscaled screenshot. Games that follow their window (Brawlhalla) can give paired
  captures of a paused scene by grabbing it at 1280×800 and at 1920×1200. Kodak stays as a
  labelled photo track (Pillow bicubic is a = −0.5; PyTorch's is −0.75, so never mix them).
- **Measure reconstruction and sharpening separately** (FSR1 EASU without RCAS vs with);
  FSR1 and NIS stay in display-encoded sRGB as their vendors require; linear-light
  filtering is a separate challenger for bilinear/bicubic/Lanczos only. Add exact
  Mitchell–Netravali (B = C = 1/3) and Lanczos-2/3 as named classical challengers.
- **Champion rule:** faithful gaming first. No gate failure, within budget, then a blinded
  reference-guided two-choice test at 1:1 on the panel (full-screen A/B for whole frames,
  side-by-side crops for detail; stills and 8–10 s clips). Owner-only reviews decide
  personal preference; claims about people in general need about 15–24 viewers.
- **P1 training starts faithful:** RGB L1 on paired game data only, then one ablation
  adding a small gradient term (0.05 × first-difference L1). No GAN, perceptual or FFT
  loss in the first model: they trade faithfulness for invented detail, which a live
  game's HUD and outlines cannot afford.

## Phases

The active ordering is in [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md#milestone-order): organization,
BUF plus finished UI, BUFP, bounded BUNet qualification, shared motion, BUFT, and
BUFG (offline first, then live). BUNet is not a technical prerequisite for motion
or generation. Keep one active production milestone and one bounded supporting
research question; each ends with qualification evidence, a usable feature, or a
documented stop decision.

Historical phase names **P0–P5** remain valid identifiers in existing specs, plans
and receipts: P0 foundation, P1 BUNet, P2 motion, P3 offline generation, P4 live
generation/pacing, P5 temporal upscaling. Preserve those identifiers rather than
renaming prior experiments. They no longer determine the current priority order.

Research basis: `../BasicUpscaler Research/Pipeline Research/BasicUpscaler_Rendering_Research_2026-09-23/modules/`
— read before starting a phase: P1 → 10, 13; P2/P5 → 14, 15; P3 → 15, 21; P4 → 01, 16, 17;
live/capture → 08, 12; measurement → 22. Image quality (what "good" means, metrics,
charts, review, losses): `../BasicUpscaler Research/Image Quality/` — 01 vision, 02
measurement, 03 retargeting and natural aspect fill, 04 sampling, reconstruction and
perceived clarity — read before any fill, arena or P1 work. All of it is theory and
prior-project cautions, not measured results; the arena decides.

## Training and GPU rules (adopted from Absolute Laya, starts in P1)

This laptop hard-powered off three times under sustained stock-clock training (Laya
`docs/UNDERVOLT_LOG.md`). Laya's validated point is a 1650 MHz cap with +300 MHz offset
via G-Helper: −26% energy per step, 64 W peak, thermal margin ≥ 9 °C, no pauses.

1. **Thermal guard on every training run:** NVML hotspot T.Limit margin sampled every
   100 ms; pause between steps below 8 °C margin until 14 °C; abort if the monitor dies.
   Port `lab/energy.py`. Validate any clock/voltage change with a real training step, not
   a matmul probe (1800/+400 passed the probe and crashed training).
2. **VRAM planning from Windows counters,** not `torch.cuda.mem_get_info` (WDDM misreports):
   PDH dedicated/shared usage per process, 0.75 GiB reserve, `set_per_process_memory_fraction`,
   measured activation peak per patch size. Port `lab/trainer.py:72-129`.
3. **OOM backoff without changing the gradient:** on a backward OOM, clear and replay the
   step with 0.7× pixels per micro-batch, same effective batch; an OOM inside the
   optimizer step aborts the run (it corrupts state).
4. **One GPU job at a time,** and training yields while a game is running.
5. **bf16 autocast** with fp32 weights; checked against fp32 on arena metrics before use.
6. **Reproducible receipts:** hashes of dataset split, augmentations, architecture, code
   and environment in each run; report seed variance rather than single runs.
7. **Resumable checkpoints** (optimizer, scheduler, RNG, epoch) separate from the lean
   export checkpoint; bounded lazy image/video loading within 16 GB RAM.
8. **Benchmark like Laya's `scripts/bench.py`:** warm up at the real size, time with GPU
   events, report p50/p95 and resident + peak VRAM with a game running.

## Rules

- Research lives in `arena/` until it wins; the app only receives promoted algorithms.
- Docs: `ROADMAP.md` owns priorities; this page owns engineering contracts; `docs/README.md` indexes evidence and `docs/PROJECT-STRUCTURE.md` defines ownership. Preserve `DECISIONS.md`, feature research ledgers, existing specs/plans, `DESIGN.md` + `PRODUCT.md` + `.impeccable/` (UI context), generated `SCOREBOARD.md`, and README responsibilities. Avoid parallel backlogs and editable copies.
- Heavy rigor for quality and latency claims; ordinary tests for plumbing.
- Datasets, runs and weights stay out of git (`data/`, `runs/`, `models/weights/`).

# Decisions

Short entries; newest last. Each: decision, why, what would change it.

1. **Restart instead of continuing "The Basic Upscaler".** The old repo shipped a working
   capture/output core but spent most effort on research and process without a loop that
   produced gains. Proven pieces are ported (D3D11 transport, pinned FSR1/NIS shaders and
   their exactness fixture); the rest stays in the old repo as reference.
2. **Rust + D3D11 for capture, processing and output; `windows` crate pinned at 0.52.0.**
   Same stack and version as the proven old code, so ports are near-verbatim. Upgrade the
   crate as one mechanical change when a needed API is missing.
3. **Media Foundation for video decode/encode.** Hardware decode and NVENC with textures
   staying on the GPU; no FFmpeg DLLs to ship. FFmpeg stays a test-only tool.
4. **Models: PyTorch for training, ONNX export, Windows ML / ONNX Runtime with the
   TensorRT-RTX execution provider (DirectML fallback).** Decided now, verified by the P1
   timing spike; change only if that spike loses.
5. **Latency is measured as a software difference, not in photons.** Added delay =
   (source present → our output displayed) − (source present → source displayed), both
   from PresentMon on the same panel, so panel delay cancels. WGC timestamps are not used.
6. **Live output is a click-through, non-activating, topmost overlay on the game's
   monitor.** The game keeps focus and input. For mouse games the real cursor is clipped to
   the game's client area and hidden. Windows 11 26200 suppresses WGC's cursor when
   `MagShowSystemCursor(FALSE)` is active, so live disables WGC cursor capture and
   composites one cached BGRA cursor at the mapped hotspot (legacy monochrome
   cursors are converted; inversion pixels become opaque white). Layered alpha-255
   flip-discard presentation and cross-process click-through are verified on this
   panel; requesting `IsBorderRequired(false)` removes the yellow capture border.
   Foreground loss pauses output and restores clip, visibility and optional
   mouse-speed matching; Ctrl+Alt+F12, Ctrl+C, source closure and guard unwinding
   restore them on exit. `bu windows` selects sources; `bu grab` writes client-only
   numbered PNGs. Live marker logs use a four-slot nonblocking staging ring; missing
   or not-yet-readable markers are -1, never matched to a different presented frame.
7. **Arena ground truth for P0: native-resolution captures downscaled in Python.** Game
   frames rendered at low resolution alias differently; paired in-game captures at two
   resolutions are added in P1.
8. **Desktop app: Slint, in the same process as the engine, in this workspace.** Light
   (one small native binary, no web runtime) and a modern look without custom drawing.
   The old named-pipe engine/client split is dropped: the app calls the same `bu-win`
   functions as the CLI, on worker threads, and stopping the app stops scaling.
9. **Training and GPU management follow Absolute Laya's measured practice** (PLAN.md,
   "Training and GPU rules"): thermal guard, Windows-counter VRAM planning, safe OOM
   backoff, one GPU job at a time, receipts. Skipped from Laya: eager data loading (our
   frame corpora don't fit in RAM), its text-specific distillation gates, torch.compile
   (no profile evidence yet).
10. **Synthetic latency qualification uses exact present identity, not nearest timestamps.**
    `bu testsource --size 1280x720 --fps 60 --seconds 20 --log source.csv` draws a
    scrolling pattern and moving bar with a 544x16 strip: white/black sync blocks,
    then 32 frame-id bits MSB first, all blocks 16x16. The fixed-size client uses a
    flip-discard swapchain, tearing where available, and a high-resolution timer.
    It ignores keyboard menu activation (Alt/F10), since a native modal menu would
    suspend this no-menu source's cadence; close/Alt+F4 still use normal handling.
    `python -m arena.latency --size 1280x720 --fps 60 --seconds 20 --method fsr1
    --out runs/latency-<timestamp>` runs native and scaled conditions, retaining
    per-process CSVs and `report.json`. `--condition native` runs the baseline
    independently. Optional `--bu` and `--presentmon` select executable paths.
    PresentMon 2.6.0 uses v1 metrics and raw QPC. A row joins only by exact PID and
    QPC inside a logged Present bracket. Repeated markers count once, at their
    earliest observed display. All source frames remain in the denominator;
    missing evidence is not claimed as a physical drop. Quantiles interpolate
    linearly across observed latencies, with added p50/p95 = scaled minus native.
    Each collector has a unique ETW session name and is stopped by that exact name.
    Diagnostic staging readback is included in scaled latency; this is software
    display timing, not photons. Since 28 Sep: `--runs N` repeats interleaved
    native/scaled pairs (single runs vary 2–18 ms with the capture phase), `--aspect`
    and `--vsync` measure the app's settings, the report records the screen refresh,
    and `bu live`'s marker rows carry FrameArrived and take times, so each result is
    split into capture, our loop, and display. Change only with a stronger identity/timing
    oracle.
11. **No game modifications; BasicUpscaler solves shape problems itself.** The owner's
    rule (28 Sep). GBFRelinkFix rendered Relink at true 16:10 but was fully reverted. For
    games locked to 16:9, Screen fill **Smart** is the default. Since 28 Sep its curve is
    the owner's pick from a blinded full-size comparison (both scenes chose a gentle curve
    over centre-exact +43% edges, uniform +11% and rigid-HUD variants): magnification
    m0 + (M − m0)·d² from the picture centre, m0 = 1 + ¾δ, M = 1 + 1.5δ, δ = canvas/image − 1
    (16:9 on 16:10: +8.3% centre, +16.7% edges), from the shapes alone. `bu_core` owns it;
    the GPU row table and pointer mapping derive from it. Settings indices stay stable
    (`screen_fill` 0 Stretch, 1 Fit, 2 Fill, 3 Blur, 4 Smart).
    Exception (owner, 29 Sep): a mod used only to collect training data is fine, e.g.
    Sparking ZERO's `Mods/CapturePause` (F8 freezes the game for `bu pair`). The shipped
    app still never needs or changes a game.
    Since 8 Oct (DECISIONS 53) this rule covers game files and mods only: BU's own run-time hooks are
    allowed for every feature.
12. **Video YCbCr→RGB runs in our shader, not Media Foundation's video processor.** The
    processor ignores `MF_MT_VIDEO_CHROMA_SITING` and misplaced decoded chroma by ~0.85
    source rows (PLAN, Known bugs). The reader delivers NV12; `yuv.rs` converts with
    MPEG-2 siting (the H.264/HEVC default), bilinear chroma, and the matrix and range the
    decoder reports (unknown: BT.709 for ≥720 rows, else BT.601). The encode side still
    uses MF's RGB→NV12 conversion until measured worse.
13. **BasicUpscaler works on every game; nothing is game-specific.** The owner's rule
    (28 Sep). No per-game profiles, tables, detection by executable name or constants
    tuned to one title. Behaviour adapts from the frames and window alone (e.g. ShapeCheck
    detects self-drawn bars; the HUD is learned from motion) and falls back to the plain
    behaviour when its evidence is weak. Models are trained across games. Advice about a
    game's own settings belongs in the README, never in code.
14. **Two baselines: FSR1 for equal inputs, FSR 3.1.5 as the reference.** The owner wants
    FSR 3.1.5 (AMD's newest non-ML upscaler) as the baseline for development and theories.
    It is temporal and needs the renderer's jittered colour, depth and motion vectors, and
    its public API is D3D12 only, so it cannot run on captured frames or in our D3D11
    engine. It runs offline in AMD's MIT research renderer Capsaicin v1.3 on scenes
    rendered as native truth, FSR 3.1.5 output and plain low-res input; BasicUpscaler is
    scored on the low-res input against both. FSR1 stays the in-app champion to beat on
    identical inputs. Results from the two are never mixed in one champion table, and any
    "FSR 3.1.5 on captured frames" run is labelled as an ablation, not FSR quality.
15. **P1 (BUNet, "BasicUpscaler Network") runs as our own D3D11 compute shaders; its size is capped at what they run fast.**
    Measured 28 Sep (PLAN, P1 timing spike): nets up to 24 channels (≈7 GMAC at 720p
    input) run in plain HLSL about as fast as PyTorch/cuDNN on tensor cores, 16×8 layers in
    1.0 ms and 24×6 in 1.6 ms, output within 1.2/255 of PyTorch. That path needs no ML
    runtime, no extra download, no D3D12 or CUDA interop and no copies, and runs on any
    D3D11 GPU. P1 therefore trains within that size (≤ 24 channels, ≤ ~1.6 ms, inside the
    3 ms budget). Tensor cores (D3D12 cooperative vectors or TensorRT-RTX) are revisited only
    if a larger net is shown to beat the capped one by a visible margin.
16. **Every BU and BUNet feature must be fast, reliable and power efficient.** The owner's
    standing rule (29 Sep), weighed in every design and review. Fast: inside the live
    budget and never adding latency. Reliable: deterministic, no flicker or popping, a
    safe fallback to the last known-good behaviour whenever a detector or model is unsure,
    and checked by gates before it goes live. Power efficient: no work without a change
    to react to (recompute on change, not per frame), no busy waits or polling, the
    fewest GPU passes (fuse resamples), and training or analysis only when the PC is
    idle and plugged in. The first feature built to it: Smart fill that keeps UI (HUD,
    menus, dialogs) at its true shape by bending the warp around it.
17. **Invent new solutions whenever they beat the known ones.** The owner's standing rule
    (29 Sep), for everything in BU and BUNet: "I am not afraid to invent new solutions if
    need be for anything we are doing." Research the state of the art first, then go past
    it where first-principles reasoning supports it. Every design panel includes a "best
    possible, from first principles" option, and judges score how far each design can go.
    New ideas are labelled as new, come with the smallest experiment that proves or kills
    them, and keep a known-good fallback, so ambition never costs DECISIONS 16 (fast,
    reliable, power efficient).
18. **BUNet phase 1a owner decisions (29 Sep).** (a) The FSR1 port test runs per stage:
    EASU and RCAS each match the GPU within 1 code on ≥ 99.99% of pixels when fed the GPU's
    own previous stage (the app's pixel shaders); the `bu image` end-to-end match is reported,
    not gated, because float rounding alone moves it ~1.2e-4 even for a correct port.
    (b) The owner's games run under the 1650 MHz training cap, so BUNet's capped timing is the
    in-game number. (c) The sealed fifth game is Terraria (pixel art, offline), if it follows
    its window. Update 30 Sep: Terraria (fixed pixel scale) and Bloons TD 6 (fixed render
    resolution) do not follow their windows; the owner chose **Monster Hunter World**
    instead (to be installed), if it passes the window and real-render checks. Capture
    only, so its anti-tamper does not matter. Training (phase 1b) does not wait for it.
    (d) The unpaired probe set is ≥ 6 games (the games the owner has), not the spec's ≥ 10;
    the generalisation check is weaker but real.
19. **BUNet phase 1b pre-registration (30 Sep, controller under the owner's delegation, O7).**
